title.text: Stablecoin Yields Under Threat and Circle Plunges 22%

spans.text: Circle, the issuer of the USDC stablecoin, suffered its worst drop since June 2025 this Tuesday. Shares
plunged 22%
following the release of a new draft of the CLARITY Act, a U.S. bill that, if passed,
would prohibit yield payments on stablecoin balances.
Coinbase, which shares revenue with Circle, fell 8% in the same trading session.
What Happened

The new draft of the CLARITY Act, legislation that seeks to regulate stablecoins in the United States, brought a significant change: the prohibition of any form of yield that is "economically equivalent to interest" on stablecoin balances. In practice, this would directly hit
Circle's
business model, which collects interest on USDC reserve assets and passes part of that revenue to
Coinbase
, which in turn offers yields to users holding USDC on the platform.

Dan Dolev, an analyst at Mizuho, explained that "the CLARITY Act could potentially ban yield payments for simply holding a stablecoin and restrict any approach that makes the program equivalent to a bank deposit." The drop came after a significant rally: Circle shares had risen over 170% since early February, leaving the stock vulnerable to any negative news.
To make matters worse, Circle also froze the USDC of 16 wallets linked to a sealed civil case in the U.S., reigniting the debate over centralization and censorship power in stablecoins.
Why This Matters

Yield on stablecoins is one of the main attractions for users and institutional investors. Removing this possibility makes it harder for tokens like USDC to evolve beyond simple payment tools. As Shay Boloor, chief strategist at Futurum Equities, put it: "This weakens a core part of the investment thesis," limiting USDC's path to becoming a true store-of-value instrument.

The impact goes beyond Circle. Coinbase derives about 20% of its revenue from USDC, and a significant portion is paid out as rewards. Robinhood (HOOD) also fell 4.7%. The broader crypto market felt the pressure: Bitcoin, which was already trading lower on the day, briefly lost the $69K level before recovering to
on news of a possible ceasefire with Iran later in the afternoon.
What's Next

Analysts at Clear Street and Bitwise consider the reaction was overblown. Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street, stated that "the actual situation doesn't look as bad as the headline suggests." Ryan Rasmussen from Bitwise pointed out that Circle is still up over 30% for the year, even after the drop, and that "there will be ways to work around" the restriction.

Meanwhile, Tether hired one of the Big Four to conduct the first full audit of USDT reserves, which, if successful, could improve the institutional image of its rival and further pressure Circle's position in the stablecoin market. The final text of the CLARITY Act may still change, but Washington's message is clear: stablecoins that function like bank deposits will face restrictions.
